11029-american-hero-myths-a-study-in-the:
Daniel G. Brinton, physician and member of the American Philosophical Society, wrote this 1882 study of Native American hero myths. Brinton argues that stories told by widely separated tribes, in different languages, are myths, not history, and must not be used to trace migrations as if hero-gods were tribal chiefs. He applies comparative methods with care, warning against turning every legend into a light or storm myth.

Quetzalcoatl, the feathered serpent of Mexico, figures largely, with temples, codices, and astrological signs examined for what they reveal about religion. Brinton's book helped found the comparative study of American religions, treating Native beliefs as systems of thought worthy of serious analysis. Modern readers should note its Victorian language and theories, now much revised.
12146-discoveries-in-australia-volume-2-:
Commander J. Lort Stokes published this second volume in 1846, reporting the survey voyage of HMS Beagle along Australian coasts from 1837 to 1843. Sent by the Admiralty, the ship charted harbors, rivers, and reefs that charts of the day left blank or wrong.

Stokes describes leaving Port Essington, working up the Victoria River, and crossing to the Gulf of Carpentaria, with notes on tides, shoals, and the search for fresh water. He also records meetings with Aboriginal people, their languages, tools, and customs, and Captain Owen Stanley visits to islands in the Arafura Sea. The volume pairs hard survey detail with first-hand scenes of a coast Europeans were only beginning to map.
13040-the-prose-works-of-jonathan-swift-:
Volume ten of Jonathan Swift's prose works, edited by Temple Scott in 1902 for Bohn's Standard Library, gathers his historical writings. The editor weighs a newly collated manuscript of Swift's History and notes its differences from the Lucas version. Lord Orrery's 1752 Remarks on Swift, which drew sharp censure from Swift's living friends, also comes under review.

Treaty terms and war politics fill the historical matter, from French fortress demolitions to the Rhine, the Treaty of Ryswyck, and the claims of Prussia and Orange. The volume matters as a scholarly record of Swift the political writer, not just the satirist.
13714-talbot-mundy-biblio-materials-towa:
Materials toward a bibliography of Talbot Mundy, edited by Bradford M. Day, gathers the facts of a wandering author's life and work. Mundy was born in London in 1879 and schooled at Rugby. He spent nearly ten years from 1900 as a government official in Africa and India, riding across India on horseback and even into Tibet.

The book lists his novels and magazine stories, with publishers, dates, and notes on first appearances, from The Marriage of Meldrum Strange to The Nine Unknown and the Tros of Samothrace serials. A short life sketch explains his pull toward Eastern occult lore and African nature magic. For collectors and readers of adventure fiction, it is the key guide to a prolific pulp author.
15130-the-fugitive-blacksmith-or-events-:
James W. C. Pennington, pastor of a Presbyterian church in New York and formerly enslaved in Maryland, tells his escape in this second edition, printed in London in 1849. He opens by thanking his publisher and the British press for calling for a new edition. An Isaiah motto on outcasts fronts the book.

Pennington recounts slavery, flight, and the building of a free life and ministry, with a blacksmith's skill at the center of his story. His voice is dignified and direct, aimed at British readers who backed abolition. The narrative stands as a strong firsthand witness to bondage, escape, and Black achievement.
15254-maxims-and-opinions-of-field-marsh:
George Henry Francis selected this 1845 volume of Wellington's maxims and opinions, drawn from his writings and speeches across more than fifty years of public life. A biographical memoir fronts the book, with a Latin motto on glory that praise cannot help nor blame harm. The editor notes that earlier books dwelt on battles.

Here the duke's political career takes its place beside his military fame, in short, pointed sayings on war, government, and character. Francis presents Wellington as a statesman as well as a soldier. Readers who like maxims and military biography will find the volume pithy, revealing, and very much of its age.
16027-journals-of-two-expeditions-of-dis:
George Grey, later governor of South Australia, published these journals in London in 1841 after two expeditions into north-west and western Australia in 1837, 1838, and 1839. Sent under government authority, Grey and his parties mapped new districts described as fertile and important, sailing by way of Tenerife, Bahia, and the Cape of Good Hope. Volume one opens with plans, instructions, and island notes.

Grey also records the moral and physical state of Aboriginal peoples he met, with vocabularies, weather tables, and notes on caves, camels, and coastal landmarks. The journals mix exploration, science, and colonial judgment in one voice. Modern readers gain a first-hand, if dated, account of how Europeans first charted Australia's remote north-west.
16145-journals-of-two-expeditions-of-dis:
Volume two of George Grey's journals, published in London in 1841, carries his Australian exploration from Gantheaume Bay toward the Hutt River and on to Perth. A second boat wrecks in Gantheaume Bay, stores are divided, and the party crosses red sandstone country, plains rich in the warran plant, and native paths and wells. Geology, scenery, and the daily grind of travel fill the chapters.

Grey, then a captain and later governor of South Australia, also notes Aboriginal people, their country, and their ways as he meets them. The journal is frank about hardship, hunger, and the limits of European knowledge in a strange land. Modern readers gain a vivid, first-hand record of mapping Western Australia's coast and interior.
16979-the-discipline-of-war-nine-address:
The Rev. J. Hasloch Potter, canon of Southwark and vicar of St. Mark's, Surbiton, wrote these nine addresses on the lessons of war in connection with Lent, issued by Skeffington in London in 1915. They run from Ash Wednesday to Easter Sunday, with an appendix giving a subject for thought and a passage of Scripture for each day in Lent. Potter says war has brought new conditions and deepened old duties.

Potter offers simple hints for conduct and points for thought, in plain, pastoral prose. He links war discipline to Lent discipline: patience, duty, and faith under strain. The book gives a clear sample of wartime church teaching, useful for readers of Great War religion and for those who study how churches spoke to a nation at war.
18720-in-the-yule-log-glow-book-i-christ:
Harrison S. Morris edited this Christmas collection for Lippincott of Philadelphia, with Book I copyrighted in 1891 and issued in a three-volumes-in-one edition in 1900. Its threshold scene gathers travelers from many lands about a Yule log, each ready to tell a native tale in turn.

Book I holds the Three Kings of Cologne from an old English chronicle, Daudet's Three Christmas Masses, Tolstoi's Russian Christmas Party, and tales from Germany, Norway, and the desert. A turkey tale, a still Christmas by Agnes Repplier, and a Norwegian tale by Björnson round out the set. The book offers fireside reading meant to carry the good cheer of Christmas across borders.
19687-the-square-of-sevens-an-authoritat:
Cartomancy is fortune-telling with ordinary playing cards. The Square of Sevens, issued in 1896, presents itself as an authoritative method of that art. Its editor praises the source text's solemn faith in its own mysteries. The old spellings and capital letters mark it as an early eighteenth-century work. Quaint phrases sit beside strict attention to business.

Books of this sort taught readers to lay cards in set patterns. Each position and card carried a fixed meaning. The square of sevens gives the method its shape. Beyond belief or doubt, the book has real literary flavor. It preserves how fortune-tellers once spoke to clients. Historians of popular magic still cite such manuals.
19830-moody-s-anecdotes-and-illustration:
Dwight L. Moody, the great revival preacher, filled sermons with stories. Moody's Anecdotes and Illustrations collects them from his revival work. The compiler kept Moody's own idiom strictly, he promises. Gold, he says, is scattered through the volume. The pieces come from Chicago tabernacle meetings and New York's Hippodrome services. Daily press reports supplied much of the text.

Moody's anecdotes were tools, not ornaments. Each short story aimed a doctrine at a hearer's conscience. Preachers mined collections like this for their own sermons. The book preserves revival preaching at its most practical. Moody's plain talk reached millions in his lifetime. These pages show the workshop behind the sermons.
20065-twenty-years-of-congress-volume-2-:
James G. Blaine wrote Twenty Years of Congress, and volume two runs from Lincoln to Garfield. It also reviews the events that led to the change of 1860. Blaine served in Congress through much of that span himself. Few men knew its fights and leaders from so close at hand.

The volume records Lincoln's death on April 15, 1865, in plain detail. Three hours later, Andrew Johnson took the oath as president. Chief Justice Chase gave that oath while the cabinet looked on. Readers get war, loss, and rebuilding told by a man who sat in the room.
20586-in-the-yule-log-glow-book-3-christ:
In the Yule-Log Glow, Book 3 gathers Christmas poems from round the world, published in 1891 as part of a set for holiday reading. The poems come from many lands and ages, all turned toward the season. Some are carols, and some are literary verses on the holy night.

One piece borrows Shakespeare's famous lines on the season. Some say that ever against the time when our Saviour's birth is celebrated, the bird of dawning sings all night long. Then no spirit dares stir abroad, and the nights are wholesome. The set was made for family reading by firelight.
21271-chocolate-or-an-indian-drinke-by-t:
Antonio Colmenero of Ledesma, a Spanish doctor, wrote this tract on chocolate. Captain James Wadsworth translated it into English for a London edition of 1652. Its title promises that wise and moderate use of the Indian drink preserves health and cures sickness, above all the plague of the guts. Beauty and easier childbirth are also claimed.

Wadsworth says the tract and the chocolate itself were first admitted to the English court under Lord Conway's patronage. The book explains the name, from Mexican words for water and the noise of stirring. It stands among the first English works promoting a drink that would reshape European habits.
21822-a-lecture-on-heads-as-delivered-by:
Heads, forty-seven of them in pictures, supply the jokes in George Alexander Stevens's famous Lecture on Heads, a one-man stage show of the 1700s. Stevens toured it through London and nearly every large town in England and Ireland to huge success. Fellow wits like Churchill and Shuter fed him new hints along the way. Later performers, Charles Lee Lewes among them, kept delivering it with additions by Mr. Pilon.

The act mocked the types of the age through carved and pictured heads, with an essay on satire added at the end. This 1812 edition answers a swarm of pirated copies that had mangled the act. It preserves a landmark of solo stage comedy, part script, part picture book.
22110-martian-v-f-w:
G. L. Vandenburg's Martian V. F. W. is a short science fiction story with a grim joke in its title. The initials twist the Veterans of Foreign Wars into veterans of a future war on Mars. His character Cruthers faces the Martians at close range. They are ants six feet tall, coloured yellow, brown, and a third bright hue, with goggle eyes that roll when they speak.

Vandenburg plays the meeting for wonder and unease at once. Earthmen who thought themselves conquerors meet beings built to unsettle them. The story appeared in the pulp magazines that fed young science fiction fans. Its brief length and sharp image are typical of that fast, idea-driven market.
26535-the-standard-electrical-dictionary:
T. O'Conor Sloane compiled this popular dictionary of words and terms used in electrical engineering, issued in 1892. Its entries run alphabetically from A to the end of the alphabet, defining the apparatus, units, and workshop terms of an industry still young. Readers meet batteries, magnets, motors, dynamos, and the many kinds of electro-magnet, each with a plain working definition.

The book predates the discovery of the electron, so its explanations of current and energy belong to an earlier physics, as the transcriber's note warns. That dated science is part of its charm for historians. For students of 1892, though, it was a desk tool, turning a fast-growing trade vocabulary into terms an amateur or workman could use.
27243-the-fulfilment-of-a-dream-of-pasto:
A. Mildred Cable's The Fulfilment of a Dream of Pastor Hsi's, published in 1917 for the China Inland Mission, tells the story of the work in Hwochow, Shansi. Cable credits co-workers Evangeline and Francesca French, superintendent Albert Lutley, and her Chinese secretary Miss Wang, who reported many interviews.

Cable warns that Shansi by itself exceeds England and Wales in size, and that one mile alters speech while ten miles change customs, so her usages are local. The book follows little Ai Do, greatly loved, and the mission's growth, in the spirit of Whitman's lines on dreams and life's love.
27288-the-life-of-trust-being-a-narrativ:
George Müller wrote this narrative of his own life, edited and condensed by Rev. H. Lincoln Wayland with an introduction by Francis Wayland, and published in Boston in 1861. Müller tells how he trusted God to provide for his orphan work at Ashley Down in Bristol, England, recording gifts, needs, and answers to prayer as they came.

The full record was far too long to reprint: the original narrative appeared in four parts between 1837 and 1856, with annual reports through 1860, filling some eighteen hundred pages. Wayland cut repeated matter to make one readable volume. Readers get a firsthand account of faith put to daily, practical use.
28320-a-tramp-s-wallet-stored-by-an-engl:
William Duthie wrote A Tramp's Wallet in 1858, dedicated by permission to Charles Dickens, as a goldsmith's wanderings in Germany and France. Duthie spent three years and a half at work and tramping, collecting facts and stray notes, sixteen chapters of which first appeared in Household Words. Darton and Company published the book in London.

Chapters cover the German workman, Hamburg to Lubeck, fair-time at Leipzig, a silver mine, Austrian jails, and German Sundays, with French workmen and jugglers. Duthie thanks Dickens for sympathy during publication. The book offers a lively, first-hand view of mid-century Europe on foot.
29047-captain-brand-of-the-centipede-a-p:
Harry Gringo, the pen name of H. A. Wise of the United States Navy, wrote this 1864 book, Captain Brand of the Centipede: A Pirate of Eminence in the West Indies. Published by Harper and Brothers in New York, it tells Brand's loves and exploits, with some account of the singular manner by which he departed this life. Wise, author of Los Gringos and Tales for the Marines, opens with verses on how God and sailors are adored in danger and slighted after.

The chapters run from spreading the strands through calm, high noon, sunset, and darkness to danger, in a pirate's life told by a naval officer. A portrait of Captain Brand fronts the book. Readers get a swashbuckling West Indian pirate tale, written with a sailor's knowledge of ships, seas, and the pirate's trade.
3098-the-paths-of-inland-commerce-a-chro:
Archer B. Hulbert argues that American history turns on transport, and this 1920 volume of the Chronicles of America series traces how trails, roads, and waterways knit the country together. Published by Yale University Press, it treats movement itself as the plot: without a way to carry goods and people inland, settlement, trade, and union would all have stalled.

Hulbert opens with a bold guess that the great American novel, if ever written, would be built around transport, since it has shaped national growth more than any single event. The chapters that follow give general readers a clear account of how routes opened the interior, linked regions, and turned a scattered set of colonies into a working continental nation.
32987-the-student-s-life-of-washington-c:
This student's life of Washington, published in New York in 1876, condenses Washington Irving's larger Life of Washington into one compact volume for young persons and schools. The publisher's note promises that all the important facts of Washington's career survive the cutting, along with the incidents that best show his character in all its aspects. Great events of the Revolutionary era are kept in proportion, not crowded out by the hero.

With illustrations, including Washington as a surveyor, the book aims to give school readers a full estimate of the man without Irving's full length. It moves from youth and surveying through command and presidency, keeping narrative and character together. As a school text of its day, it shows how nineteenth-century America taught its founding story: through a great life, told plainly and with admiration.
33148-my-first-book-the-experiences-of-w:
My First Book, edited with an introduction by Jerome K. Jerome and published in London in 1894 with 185 illustrations, gathers the experiences of twenty-one famous authors on their first books. Its contributors include Besant, Payn, Kipling, Conan Doyle, Haggard, Ballantyne, Corelli, Stevenson, and others.

Each writer tells how a first book came to be written, placed, and received, with the blunders, luck, and encouragement that shaped a career. Jerome opens the volume with a small scene about the right time, a modest start for a book about beginnings. For writers and readers, it remains a delightful, practical record of literary apprenticeship in the late Victorian age, full of candor and good stories.
33906-the-sword-of-deborah-first-hand-im:
F. Tennyson Jesse wrote this first-hand account of British women's war work in France, published in New York in 1919. Jesse follows the Women's Army Auxiliary Corps, the First Aid Nursing Yeomanry, and Voluntary Aid Detachment workers through convoys, outposts, and night duty. An epigraph from Thomas Dunn English opens the book.

Chapters move from a fever chart of war and backgrounds to brown graves, vignettes, evening, rest, and notes and queries. Jesse writes with warmth for women who did bold things in a quiet way. The book preserves a woman's view of war service close to the front.
36427-art-principles-with-special-refere:
Ernest Govett wrote Art Principles, with special reference to painting, in 1919. Putnam at New York and London put out the book that year. Thirty-one illustrations stand in it, one from Fragonard's Pursuit. Its full title adds notes on the illusions produced by the painter. An introduction defines art and beauty at the start.

Aesthetic systems, the earliest art, and art periods pass in that survey. Greek and Italian developments and the nature of genius take sections. The impressionist movement and the broad manner are weighed there too. Rembrandt and Velasquez hold their positions in art in his account. Landscape holds its own place in the same introduction. Book one classifies the fine arts and their several scopes. Relative value of form in poetry stands in his comparisons. Govett gives the painter's craft a reasoned ground plan.
38132-a-hundred-and-sixty-books-by-washi:
A Hundred and Sixty Books by Washington Authors is a reading guide compiled by Susan Whitcomb Hassell. It was printed for the compiler at Everett, Washington, in 1916. The little book sold for thirty five cents in paper and fifty in cloth. Its contents sort Washington writing by kind. History, travel, and scientific works come first in the list. Fiction, juvenile books, and poetry follow in their own sections. Unclassified prose and other periodical writers are also included.

Each entry gives a short note on the book it names. The history section opens with a pioneer home life account from 1909. A Columbia River history by a Whitman College professor follows. Lines worth knowing by heart fill the last main section. An index to writers closes the volume. The guide maps a young state's literature for its own readers.
38557-granny-s-chapters-on-scriptural-su:
Lady Mary Ross wrote Granny's Chapters on scriptural subjects, and this volume treats the New Testament, in a new edition printed at London in eighteen eighty-two. Her preface, dated November, eighteen seventy-one, says the New Testament is handled in a way unlike her Old Testament volumes. The aim is to sketch the earthly life of Christ and draw out a few great points. Ross holds that the plain words of the Gospels are best read in the Bible itself.

The first part opens with the birth of John the Baptist, son of the priest Zacharias and his wife Elisabeth. Ross sets the scene under Roman rule, with Herod set over the land by Rome. A sketch of the later history of the Jews follows the Gospel tale. The book was made to lead the young to a close study of the Saviour's life.
38609-the-corner-house-girls-on-a-houseb:
Grace Brooks Hill wrote The Corner House Girls on a Houseboat. Barse and Hopkins issued it at New York in 1920. Thelma Gooch drew its pictures. Nine Corner House books line the front. Snowbound stands just before this one in line. What's That heads the first chapter.

Neale Has News and The Elevator follow fast. The Houseboat itself enters at chapter five. Making Plans and The Robbery build the voyage. All Aboard and A Stowaway raise the fun. A Trick Mule and the circus fill the middle. Ruth's Alarm and Up the River come next. A storm and an island strand the party late. The Capture closes the twenty-fifth chapter. Ruth spots the same two men in the front plate. Sisterly adventure on the water gave girl readers a floating home and a thief hunt in one summer.
40091-the-solution-of-the-pyramid-proble:
The Solution of the Pyramid Problem, by Robert Ballard, puts a new theory of the pyramids of Egypt before the public. John Wiley and Sons issued the book at New York in 1882. Ballard was chief engineer of a railway division in Queensland, Australia. His book promises pyramid discoveries with a fresh account of their ancient use. A plate shows a plumb line set over the pyramids.

Victorian readers loved a bold key to the pyramid riddle, and Ballard offers one. He brings the measures and levels of an engineer to the stones. From those measures he draws a theory of what the great piles were for. The book belongs to the flood of pyramid studies of its age. Some were sound surveys, and some were pure fancy. Ballard writes as a practical man sure of his lines and numbers.
40236-memoirs-of-benjamin-franklin-writt:
Volume Two of the Memoirs of Benjamin Franklin, Written by Himself, was issued at New York in 1860 by Harper and Brothers. The set holds Franklin's life plus his best essays, letters, and sundry writings. The front note says the pieces were chosen with care from all his printed works. Matter that most pleases the plain reader was the aim.

Essays lead the volume with The Way to Wealth from Poor Richard. True happiness, public men, and waste of life get short pieces. Self denial, maths, sweet dreams, and health rules follow. Advice to a young tradesman and a tale of the Ephemera sit side by side. Letters and state papers fill the rest. The volume shows Franklin as sage, wit, and man of affairs.
40536-whittaker-co-s-list-of-classical-e:
Whittaker and Company List of Classical, Educational, and Technical Works is a publisher catalogue. The firm kept its shop at White Hart Street, Paternoster Square, in London. A contents page sorts the list by school subject for the browsing buyer. Atlases and arithmetic stand with Greek and Latin in that index.

Bibliotheca Classica and Cambridge Greek and Latin texts head the classical side. Grammar school classics and lower form series fill the school list in the contents. French, German, Italian, Spanish, and Russian books get sections of their own here. Euclid, science, Shakespeare, and a specialist series close the roll of subjects. Schoolmasters and booksellers ordered their year stock from lists like this one.
4061-the-fifteen-decisive-battles-of-the:
Sir Edward Creasy's history picks fifteen battles that changed the world, from Marathon to Waterloo. A sampled passage follows Hannibal's daring march, as he leaves the southern road, wheels north toward Picenum, and sends messengers with Hasdrubal's letters to the Roman senate.

Creasy argues that single days of fighting can turn the fate of nations, and he tells each battle as a story of generals, ground, and law. The book suits readers who like military history with a clear thesis, where maps and marches carry the weight of empires. Creasy writes for the general reader, not only for soldiers.
42602-the-steam-engine-explained-and-ill:
The Steam Engine Explained and Illustrated, by Dionysius Lardner, reached a seventh edition from Taylor and Walton in London in 1840. Its full title promises an account of the engine's invention and progressive improvement, and of its application to navigation and railways, with a memoir of Watt. A frontispiece engraves Watt from the statue by Chantrey.

Contents begin with preliminary matter: the power of steam, disputes over the invention, and the machine of Hero of Alexandria. Blasco de Garay's proposal to propel vessels, Solomon de Caus, Giovanni Branca's mill scheme, and the Marquis of Worcester follow in the line of claimants. Lardner then lays down the mechanical properties of fluids and the effects of heat before applying the principles to engines.
43770-gardens-of-the-caribbees-v-1-2-ske:
Ida M H Starr wrote Gardens of the Caribbees, sketches of a cruise south. L C Page and Company issued volume one at Boston in nineteen hundred three. Her ship sailed the West Indies and the Spanish Main that year. The cruise fell in the winter and spring of nineteen hundred one.

No guide book was her aim, she owns in her first kind words. The human side of each port drew her pen far more than sights. Charlotte Amalie on Saint Thomas fronts the book in a plate. Pomegranate shade and bright streets greet the new come guest there. War, fever, and revolt soon shut those ports to such gay trips. Haiti sank to riot; fevers barred snug harbours to the fleet. She counts her bright weeks as a chance that may not come again. Gay fancy is left free rein through her sun lit sketches.
43771-gardens-of-the-caribbees-v-2-2-ske:
Gardens of the Caribbees, volume two, by Ida M H Starr, was held under a 1903 copyright and printed at Boston by L C Page and Company. Starr sketches a cruise to the West Indies and the Spanish Main. The set runs to two volumes, rich with plates.

A front plate shows a view from a balcony at Caracas in Venezuela. The first chapter treats the island of Trinidad, which Starr calls by its old name, Iere. She jokes that a bit more knowledge of Trinidad would have saved a lunch that went wrong. The cruise moves on through island ports, gardens, and towns. Travel readers of 1903 got sun, sea, and colonial scenes in a chatty, pictured form.
44560-three-courses-and-a-dessert-compri:
Three Courses and a Dessert, printed in 1867, serves three sets of tales, west country, Irish, and legal, with a melange for the last course. The author is not named. Fifty pictures by George Cruikshank go with the tales. A motto from As You Like It bids the reader sit down and feed, and welcome to our table. A short induction plays host. Its writer greets his guests with a hearty but respectful welcome.

The dishes may miss one taste, he hopes, but another course will hold something sharp for each. The artist has graced his rough sketches in their transfer to wood. A bill of fare then lays out the meal. The first course, west country chronicles, gives Sir Mathew Ale, the counterpart cousins, and Caddy Cuddle. The second course turns to the neighbours of an old Irish cottage, with Jimmy Fitzgerald first.
45020-the-divining-rod-virgula-divina-ba:
Charles Latimer, a civil engineer, wrote this essay on the divining rod, printed at Cleveland in 1876. The rod is named in Latin on the title page and glossed as water-witching in plain speech. Latimer first read the essay before the Civil Engineers' Club of the Northwest, at Chicago on February 1, 1875. A line from Shakespeare heads the title page, on things undreamt of in philosophy.

In his preface Latimer says he has no apology for treating the subject in a serious light. He holds it to lie strictly in the domain of science and worthy of study by men of science. He claims to know the truth of it for himself, not from another. Notes from many sources, found after the essay was written, close the book.
45727-the-boy-aviators-with-the-air-raid:
The Boy Aviators with the Air Raiders, a story of the Great World War by Captain Wilbur Lawton, was copyrighted in 1915 by Hurst and Company of New York. Pictures by Charles L Wrenn go with the text. Lawton wrote a long line of Boy Aviators books, from Nicaragua to the polar dash. This one takes the boys to the war zone of Europe.

Frank leads the party, with Billy and Pudge, since his brother Harry lies hurt with a broken arm and collar bone. Chapters bring German spies, the saving of a great seaplane, and a night on the Channel. The boys fly under shrapnel fire, guard a windmill fort, and join the raid that bombarded Zeebrugge. A snow squall and a desperate game of tag test the Sea Eagle.
49238-a-brief-narrative-of-the-fourth-te:
George Guild wrote A Brief Narrative of the Fourth Tennessee Cavalry Regiment, published at Nashville in 1913. The regiment served in Wheeler's Corps of the Army of Tennessee, on the Confederate side of the Civil War. Portraits of its colonel, lieutenant colonel, major, and adjutant open the book.

Guild dedicates the narrative to comrades who went with the regiment but did not come back. The book records the unit's service as its survivors remembered it half a century later. Such regimental histories were often written by veterans for veterans, preserving names, marches, and fights that official reports slighted. This one keeps the memory of a Tennessee cavalry regiment in print for families and for students of the war in the West.
50253-camp-mates-in-michigan-or-with-pac:
George Rathborne wrote a boys' tale of camp life in the Michigan pine woods. Donohue of Chicago copyrighted it in 1913, in a series of canoe and campfire books. Three boys sleep in a lone tent on the bank of a Michigan stream. A shout wakes them in the dark, for some beast is after their food store.

Dolph, Teddy, and their chum seize their guns and rush out half awake. The chapters ahead promise paddling against the stream, a root hunter, and proof that talks. Game poachers, a haunted cabin, and fly fishing for bass fill the middle of the book. The boys work down the Tahquamenon and shoot the Soo Rapids at the close. Rathborne drew on long years as a sportsman, and the tale is full of woodcraft for Boy Scouts.
50919-a-bibliography-of-bibliography-or-:
Joseph Sabin made a bibliography of bibliography, a handy book about books which relate to books, printed at New York in 1877. Sabin had written a Dictionary of Books relating to America. The list runs in alphabetical order over the chief works on the literature of Great Britain and America, with more than a few on France and Germany. A soldier without arms may be valiant but not victorious, the motto warns.

To aim at learning without books is to draw water in a sieve. Sabin's preface owns the book grew from Power's Handy Book about Books, which he found wanting on a close look. His list runs about four times Power's size. Bookmen and librarians get a guide to the guides here.
5334-journals-of-two-expeditions-into-th:
John Oxley's Journals of Two Expeditions into the Interior of New South Wales, ordered by the British government in 1817 and 1818, records the surveyor general's journeys into newly discovered country. Oxley, a lieutenant of the Royal Navy, travelled with maps and views of the interior, corrected in this text from twelve items of errata in the original.

The journals follow two expeditions through rivers, plains, and unknown lands, with notes in square brackets and illustrations omitted here. Readers get a primary record of early Australian exploration, in which a surveyor measured a continent that Europeans were only beginning to understand.
54079-sinners-and-saints-a-tour-across-t:
Phil Robinson, who wrote In My Indian Garden and Under the Punkah, made this tour of America. Sinners and Saints came out in a new, cheaper edition at London in 1892. The subtitle adds a draw: three months among the Mormons.

From New York to Chicago opens the road, by the Pennsylvania Limited. Robinson notes street scenes, stockyards, and merry-makers on the way. Chicago to Denver crosses the great rivers and the prairies, past Omaha and Council Bluffs. In Leadville he finds busted lords of mines and the creed of thick boots. Jokes and sharp eyes mark the whole ride, in the manner of a man used to sizing up strange lands.
56267-the-game-fish-of-the-northern-stat:
The Game Fish of the Northern States and British Provinces is an angling book by Robert Barnwell Roosevelt, printed at New York in 1884. Roosevelt also wrote Superior Fishing and The Game Birds of the North. A portrait of the author fronts the volume. Its title promises the salmon and sea-trout fishing of Canada and New Brunswick.

Simple directions for tying artificial flies stand among its extras. The preface is wry: Roosevelt has said in his first paragraph that a preface is a sort of apology. His apology here is that demand for a new edition seemed so large he ought to comply. A great deal of fresh matter was added, and the information brought down to the present time. He calls the work a labour of love, and praises out-door recreation as a national good. The book is a founding text of American sport fishing.
56934-the-venus-of-milo-an-archeological:
Paul Carus wrote a study of the famed Venus of Milo and her cult. The book came out in Chicago in 1916 with plates. Carus frames her as the goddess of womanhood in full. A Homeric hymn line in Greek heads the book. The find of the statue leads the tale.

A sea man's report and a count's own tale tell of the find. A drawn form by Debay shows one view of her shape. Carus then sets out her form, lost arms, and fix tries. What the facts show is weighed with care in the mid part. Aphrodite's name, cult, and war side close the book. Art fans get lore and looks in one store.
58695-whale-primer-with-special-attentio:
Whale Primer, with special attention to the California gray whale, by Theodore J Walker, was published by the Cabrillo Historical Association in 1962. The book was produced with the National Park Service. It went through four printings by 1969. The gray whale, Walker writes, had become a major tourist attraction in southern California, and the primer answers the public's questions about it.

Two migration routes open the book, with the summer and winter whale waters. Filter whales and their feeding come next, then the evolution of whales and their fitting for the sea. Blubber gets a chapter for its work in warmth, floating, and food storage. The gray whale itself is treated at length: its place, range, shore habits, and answer to whaling. A last part tells the history of whaling and the protection of the gray whale.
6053-evelina-or-the-history-of-a-young-l:
Fanny Burney's Evelina, or The History of a Young Lady's Entrance into the World, appeared in 1778 and opens with an inscription to her father, Dr. Burney. She calls him author of her being, dearer than light, nourishment, or rest, and credits his example for any love of virtue glowing in her heart.

If her weak powers cannot trace his virtues, she asks concealment as her only boon, and begs him to accept the tribute and forget the lines' folly. The novel that follows sends a young lady into London society, where manners, suitors, and assemblies test her. Burney writes with wit about a girl learning the world.
62705-the-book-of-nature-containing-info:
Book of Nature is a frank guide to sex and child bearing for the young. James Ashton, a doctor and lecturer on sexual physiology, wrote it. Wallis and Ashton published it in New York in the year 1861. Its title page promises the philosophy of procreation in plain terms. It also pledges rules to prevent conception and to manage labour.

An index lists the organs of generation, the signs of pregnancy, and like topics. Labour and child birth fill the last stretch of the short book. Drugs, coverings, and ergot of rye each get their own entries. Ashton also sold a device he calls the Reveil Nocturne in the book. Few books of its day spoke so plainly to young couples.
77487-the-treatment-of-nature-in-english:
Myra Reynolds wrote The Treatment of Nature in English Poetry Between Pope and Wordsworth, issued at Chicago by the University of Chicago Press in 1909. The book runs to nearly four hundred pages with a bibliographical index. Its chapters open with nature in English classical poetry, then trace signs of a new attitude toward nature in the verse of the eighteenth century. Fiction, travels, gardening, and landscape painting each get a chapter in turn.

Plates show Longleate and Hagley Park, a portrait by Lely, Mrs Carnac by Sir Joshua Reynolds, and Squire Hallett and his wife by Gainsborough. Reynolds argues from verse, novels, travel books, gardens, and pictures together that feeling for wild and plain nature grew through the century. The study is a work of scholarship on how English taste in landscape changed before Wordsworth.
8820-a-treasury-of-war-poetry-british-an:
George Herbert Clarke, professor of English at the University of Tennessee. Edited this Riverside Literature Series treasury of British and American poems of the World War, covering 1914 to 1917. The American section opens with Kipling's The Choice, Henry van Dyke on liberty enlightening the world. Robert Bridges to the United States, Vachel Lindsay's Abraham Lincoln walking at midnight. Jeanne Robert Foster on the William P. Frye. England and America follow, with Florence Holt, Charles Langbridge Morgan, Helen Gray Cone, and Hardwicke Rawnsley at St Paul's.

Clarke's introduction and notes frame the poems as literature and as testimony, chosen while the war still raged. The anthology captures early wartime feeling: idealism, grief, and alliance, before disillusion set in. Readers of First World War poetry will find famous names beside forgotten ones. A snapshot of how Americans and Britons first versified a war they were still fighting.
8909-the-system-of-nature-or-the-laws-of:
Paul Henri Thiry, Baron d'Holbach, argues materialism and atheism in The System of Nature, first published in French in 1770 under the pseudonym of Mirabaud. This volume, translated by Samuel Wilkinson from the 1820-21 English edition, covers the first of the original two books, with an introduction by Robert D. Richardson Jr. Part one treats laws of nature, of man, and of the moral and physical world, in a system that denies miracles, spirits, and divine providence.

D'Holbach's case, that matter in motion explains mind, morals, and society, shocked Europe and influenced later freethought and radical politics. The book's plain, relentless argument made it a byword for atheism in its century. Readers of Enlightenment philosophy will find a landmark text, best read beside Voltaire, Diderot, and the Encyclopedists, and still provocative in its claim that nature needs no author outside itself.
8910-the-system-of-nature-or-the-laws-of:
First printed in French in 1770 under the name of Mirabaud, this work is in truth by Baron d'Holbach, a leading voice of the French Enlightenment. This file holds the second of its two volumes, in an English version from 1820-21. It takes on claims about God, the soul, and fate, and sets out a view of the world run by matter and law alone.

Chapters test proofs put forth by Clarke, Descartes, and Newton, and weigh ideas such as pantheism, theism, and final causes. D'Holbach argues that fear and false notions of gods harm human joy, and that reason and nature should guide morals instead. The book remains a bold, plain statement of atheist thought in its age.
9562-barclay-of-ury-and-other-poems-part:
Part three of Whittier's Narrative and Legendary Poems gathers more of his tales in verse, led by Barclay of Ury. Barclay, a Scots soldier turned Quaker, bore mob scorn with patience and noble soul, finding honor in meekness. The part also holds The Angels of Buena Vista, The Legend of St. Mark, and The Gift of Tritemius. Whittier pairs history with moral force in each compact tale.

Later poems range from Skipper Ireson's Ride and The Pipes at Lucknow to Telling the Bees and The Swan Song of Parson Avery. Each tale turns on duty, faith, or fate, in plain, stirring verse. A reader gets another rich slice of Whittier's narrative art, where old legends teach new courage.
9783-female-scripture-biography-volume-i:
Volume two of Francis Augustus Cox's Female Scripture Biography, printed in Boston in 1831, continues his lives of Bible women. Cox's preface quotes The Ladies' Calling: women deserve higher thoughts of themselves, not the world's injurious estimates. God and nature, he holds, barred women from no noble pursuit. The volume pairs the lives with his essay on what Christianity has done for women.

Like volume one, this book presents scriptural heroines as models of faith, courage, and worth, for devotional reading. Cox writes with earnest respect for his subjects. A reader gets a further set of early Victorian women's religious lives, and a companion to the first volume's portraits.
a-treasury-of-war-poetry-british-and-ame: George Herbert Clarke edits this treasury of war poetry, gathering British and American poems of the World War from 1914 to 1917. The contents open with America: Kipling's Choice, Van Dyke on liberty enlightening the world, Bridges to the United States, and Lindsay's Lincoln walking at midnight. England, England and America, and France follow, with Newbolt, Galsworthy, Seaman, Chesterton, and Van Dyke among the voices of nations at war.
american-hero-myths-a-study-in-the-nativ: Daniel Garrison Brinton studies American hero-myths in the native religions of the western continent, building on his earlier Myths of the New World. He compares the sacred stories of Indigenous peoples, seeking shared patterns in their heroes and gods. Dedicated to Eli Price, the book is a pioneering work of American comparative mythology.
barclay-of-ury-and-other-poems-part-3-fr:
John Greenleaf Whittier's narrative and legendary poems form this third part of the first volume of his works. Barclay of Ury leads: Robert Barclay, an old soldier of Gustavus Adolphus turned Quaker convert, bore the mob's indignities with a nobleness that shamed his persecutors. Whittier, himself a Friend, honours the patience of the once proud gentleman.

The Angels of Buena Vista, The Legend of St Mark, and Kathleen follow. New England pieces include Skipper Ireson's Ride, The Sycamores, and Telling the Bees, while The Pipes at Lucknow carries the Indian Mutiny. Maud Muller appears among the texts, sighing that she might have been the Judge's bride after their hayfield meeting. Legend, history, and Quaker testimony blend in Whittier's storytelling verse, much of it written for abolition-era magazines.
britannica-1911-sydney-n-s-w:
Sydney, capital of New South Wales in Australia, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands in Cumberland county on the east coast of the continent. The city sits on the south shore of Port Jackson. Few capitals in the world can match Sydney in natural gains and beauty of site, the entry holds.

It rests on rolling and well drained ground above a bed of sandstone rock. That ground juts as a peninsula into one of the deepest and safest harbours in the world. A great coal bearing area also lies at its centre as a boon. The urban area forms a peninsula about thirteen miles long between two rivers. Its sea front runs twelve miles from the South Head of Port Jackson to Botany Bay. Bold cliffs trade places with fine beaches along that shore.
britannica-1911-wellington-n-s-w: Wellington, a town in Wellington county, New South Wales, is noted in a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It lies north west of Sydney by rail, a trip of two hundred forty eight miles. In nineteen oh one it had just under three thousand folk. A fine rail bridge spans the Macquarie river there. Rich gold reefs lie nearby, and gold dredging is a growing trade. Wheat is the main farm crop, and fruit trees and vines do well.
discoveries-in-australia-volume-2-discov:
The northern coasts of Australia fill Stokes's second volume, printed at London in 1846. Contents for the opening chapter list Port Essington, Clarence Strait, Shoal Bay, and Port Darwin. Mosquitoes and sandflies, a large ant's nest, and the country's parched look stand in the same list.

Native visits get close note: teeth perfect, rites, and modes of getting water where salt water is drunk. A theory of an inland sea and a central desert is weighed. The Victoria River and the Gulf of Carpentaria fill later chapters. A view inland shows a vast plain with clumps of small trees, and gums behind a fringe of mangroves. The volume is survey narrative, chart by chart.
doe-osti-2566160-brochure-for-the-doe-of:
A short brochure prepared for the Department of Energy Office of Science sums up the February 2025 workshop Envisioning Frontiers in AI and Computing for Biological Research. The computing and biology programs ran it jointly, and Daniela Ushizima, Christopher Henry, Prasanna Balaprakash, and colleagues organized the work. Its theme is transforming bioscience with artificial intelligence, machine learning, digital twins, and high-performance computing.

Attendees from plant science, microbiology, mathematics, computer science, and AI weighed the state of the field. The workshop closed with four priority research directions. The first targets data fusion, joining scattered data sets so processes can be traced from molecules to whole-organism traits. Other themes include automated laboratories that feed results back into models, and engineering new functions into plants and microbes. The brochure frames the directions as a guide for future research inside the Office of Science.
doe-osti-2572341-analyzing-multifaceted-:
Final technical report DE-SC0019039, led by Joshua A. Levine at the University of Arizona from September 2018 to August 2024, develops topological analytics for complex scientific data. Many data sets carry several fields at once, and no single view shows their structure. The project paired topology, which maps a field's shape through its level sets, with machine learning, letting each cover the other's weaknesses.

Three thrusts organize the results. The first built ways to compare shapes, including a stable distance between merge trees and a survey of metrics on Reeb graphs. The second fed topological features straight into learning pipelines, such as clustering point clouds by their persistence diagrams. The third pioneered implicit neural representations of data. Much of the software landed in the Topological ToolKit, an open-source package that brings these methods into the ParaView analysis platform.
doe-osti-2574133-marsame-release-report-:
Release report LA-UR-25-27390, revision 2, by Mary Jo Chastenet and Jamie Lynn Gerard and issued July 25, 2025, documents a radiological survey at Los Alamos. Replacement water lines were run between Technical Areas 48 and 55. Before the disturbed soil could be released, it had to be checked for radioactive contamination under the MARSAME survey protocol, the federal standard for such decisions.

A characterization survey came first, sampling surface soil and sediment across the project area. Visual Sample Plan software set the sampling grid, landing near twenty-four samples per decision unit with error rates fixed at five and ten percent. Some points moved for fences, concrete, or rough ground. Results were compared against background values for uranium and other isotopes. The report lays out the disposition paths that follow from the numbers, from landfill release below background to controlled handling above authorized limits.
doe-osti-2583237-october-2024-semiannual:
Savannah River National Laboratory report SRNL-STI-2025-00170, by K. A. Hill and M. C. Hsieh in August 2025, files the October 2024 semiannual leaching results for salt waste grout. The Salt Waste Processing Facility's decontaminated salt solution is sampled twice a year before transfer to the Saltstone Production Facility, where it is mixed into grout and disposed of on site.

For this round, one waste form sample was made in the laboratory from the facility's waste acceptance sample plus Z-area premix. The mix used a cement-free grout recipe, sixty percent slag to forty percent fly ash by weight. After sixty-four days of curing, the sample went to a certified laboratory for the Toxicity Characteristic Leaching Procedure, the standard test for whether a waste counts as hazardous. The sample met South Carolina's hazardous waste rules for a non-hazardous waste form, the report concludes.
doe-osti-2590044-multiphysics-modeling-o:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL/NEAMS-25/2 reviews fiscal year 2025 microreactor modeling with the NEAMS code family. Authors Yinbin Miao, Soon Kyu Lee, Kevin Sawatzky, and co-authors link separate codes into one framework. Griffin handles neutron behavior, BISON heat and mechanics, Sockeye heat pipes, and SAM coolant loops. Three reactor styles are modeled, plus the KRUSTY test reactor for checking results.

A sodium heat-pipe variant was rebuilt to match recently validated heat-pipe experiments, becoming the main model for that line. Load-following runs and a single heat-pipe failure case were repeated on it, showing the expected self-limiting temperature response. Adding a hydrogen migration model raised the computed reactivity by about 600 parts per million against a flat-profile run. The report shows the tool chain handling full cores, not just single parts.
doe-osti-3001411-toward-drilling-the-per:
Adam Schultz of Oregon State University leads the EDGE project in the final technical report for award DE-EE0008793, covering October 2019 to December 2023, filed August 2025. Geothermal wells cost too much to drill, and failures are expensive; this international coordination network attacked both with data. The stated ambition was cutting drilling costs by up to seventy percent while predicting trouble before it strands a well.

A repository gathered records from over one hundred geothermal wells across varied geology, structured and unstructured, organised under FAIR principles with provenance and quality control. Cloud pipelines fed machine learning workflows that forecast rate of penetration, non-productive time and total cost, using methods such as self-organising maps. Exploratory analysis graded the incoming data's quality, an unglamorous step the report treats as foundational. Probabilistic models and adaptive planning tools round out the framework, pointing toward drilling programmes that learn from every well ever drilled.
doe-osti-3002053-measurement-of-amli-sou:
Robert Bean of Oak Ridge National Laboratory measures new neutron sources in ORNL/SPR-2025/4235, dated September 2025. The sources use americium and lithium, called AmLi sources, and came from Savannah River National Laboratory. They will serve in the LV-AWCC, an instrument that counts neutrons to assay uranium-bearing items. Such counting supports nuclear material accounting.

Bean compared the new sources against two existing Oak Ridge source sets. The new set's neutron count rate fell within 4 percent of one Oak Ridge set. It ran 40 percent higher than the other set. On that basis, counting times for uranium items should stay about the same, and may drop against one set. The report adds that total measurement uncertainty still needs further work.
doe-osti-3005271-life-cycle-cost-analysi:
Abigail G. King, Douglas B. Elliott, and Kelsey A. Semrod of Pacific Northwest write a how-to framework for the Federal Energy Management Program, dated August 2025. Federal law requires agencies to run a life-cycle cost analysis before water efficiency projects. Many project officers are not economists, so this framework standardizes the math: initial investment, operations, maintenance, replacement, and disposal, all in present value.

The method compares a base case against alternatives on equal footing. Cost lines include energy, water and wastewater bills, installation, and upkeep. Water price escalation rates from a 2023 companion study feed the forecasts. Building life-cycle cost software from the Energy Department supports the calculations. The framework's promise is mundane but valuable: two agencies pricing similar projects should reach comparable answers.
doe-osti-3019339-report-on-coastal-struc:
Ben McGilton, Kelly Gjestvang, Katie Peterson, and six colleagues at the National Laboratory of the Rockies assessed wave energy built into coastal structures in NLR/TP-5700-90768, February 2026. Coastal structure integrated wave energy converters bolt power takeoff onto breakwaters and seawalls. The host structure already faces the waves; the converter harvests them. Device families in the survey include oscillating water columns and overtopping designs such as the Seawave Slotcone Generator. Cost tables compare structure types, from gabions to reinforced concrete and sheetpile.

Integration changes the economics of both partners. The breakwater gains a revenue stream, and the converter skips building a foundation in the surf. Structural response under wave loading gets its own treatment, drawn from published device studies. For port authorities weighing a breakwater rebuild, the report offers a catalog of what could be embedded. It also flags the added loads and maintenance questions that come with the bargain.
doe-osti-3684121-development-and-validat: Lawrence Livermore document LLNL-TR-2023569, dated September 2026, is a single SULI peer review of a student poster. Sarasvati Satyanarayana reviewed Gillian Woo's project, with Corie Horwood also named on the cover. Woo converted MATLAB scripts for a ZYGO interferometer into Python and expanded them. The tool aligns laser scans of both faces of a thin film to find thickness, flatness, and parallelism. The review praises the clear layout and deep grasp of the code. It notes one gap: more background on why flatness matters for National Ignition Facility targets.
doe-osti-3685160-october-2025-semiannual:
Savannah River report SRNL-STI-2026-00224, dated July 2026, gives leach test results for an October 2025 salt waste sample. Madison Hsieh and Katie Hill are the printed authors. The Salt Waste Processing Facility sends cleaned salt solution to the Saltstone plant, where it is grouted for disposal. Twice a year, a composite sample goes through the Toxicity Characteristic Leaching Procedure. That test checks whether cured grout leaks harmful metals.

The October sample used a cement-free grout mix of slag and fly ash, in a sixty-to-forty blend by weight. After fifty-one days of curing, the sample went to a certified lab. Results met the rules for a non-hazardous waste form on regulated metals and other listed constituents. They also met the Saltstone plant's waste acceptance limits in force when the sample was taken. Mercury in the leach stayed far under its limit.
doe-osti-3883787-development-and-validat:
Livermore report LLNL-TR-2023876, dated September 2026, documents a Python rewrite of a film-thickness analysis workflow. The title page credits S. Ravandi and G. Woo, and the abstract speaks in the voice of SULI intern Gillian Woo. Target fabrication for the National Ignition Facility depends on exact measures of thin, delicate films. A ZYGO interferometer maps each film's two faces with white light, and older MATLAB code turned those maps into thickness values. The intern's tool replaces that path with open-source Python.

The software computes thickness, flatness, and parallelism from surface-height data. Three fiducial markers on each scan let it shift the bottom face into line with the top. A region picked on one face maps to the same spot on the other. The tool now serves two substrate families, with more planned. Woo notes using a lab AI assistant for parts of the code.
evelina-or-the-history-of-a-young-lady-s:
Evelina, or the History of a Young Lady's Entrance into the World, by Fanny Burney and dated 1778, is the novel that made its young author famous overnight. Burney published it without her name and prefaced it with verses to her father, Dr Burney, calling him the author of her being and the school of her virtues. The book itself is written in letters, Evelina's own, sent home from her first season among strangers.

Raised in retirement by a guardian, Evelina Anville comes to London with beauty, no experience, and a birth secret that touches her right to the name she bears. Balls, operas, and pleasure gardens expose her to rakes, fops, and one grave lord whose opinion she learns to value. Burney writes comedy of manners from inside a girl's embarrassment, and her satire of mothers, captains, and dancing masters set the pattern for the English novel of manners.
female-scripture-biography-volume-ii-inc:
Cox brings his lives of Bible women to a close in Female Scripture Biography, Volume II. Francis Augustus Cox wrote both volumes, and this Boston edition is dated 1831. The set pairs the lives with an essay on what Christianity has done for women. A contents list at the front maps the first volume's ground, from the Virgin Mary and Eve onward.

The second volume dwells on the women of the Gospels. The sampled pages sit with Mary and Martha, the sisters of Bethany. Cox praises the choice of Mary, who sat at the feet of Jesus, and finds rest for the soul in her obedience. He then turns to the sisters' trials, and notes how fast joy and pain follow each other in a human life. The tone stays warm and pastoral to the end.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BoxleyWilliamMe:
Harold Weisberg wrote this memorandum on December 7, 1968, about the reports and memos of investigator William Boxley. Weisberg, the dean of Kennedy assassination researchers, kept written assessments of the people working the same ground he did.

The memo comments on Boxley's reports, including his claims about the 'true head' of the National States Rights Party, a far-right group that figured in the era's investigations. Weisberg was famously combative about other investigators' work, and his memos grade their leads without mercy. The memo survives in his files as part of the assassination movement's internal record.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DeSlatteOscarW_:
On May 2, 1967, Assistant District Attorney James L. Alcock sent a memorandum to his boss, New Orleans District Attorney Jim Garrison. Garrison was then running his own investigation into President Kennedy's assassination. Alcock's memo records an interview with Fred A. Sewell, fleet manager of a New Orleans Chevrolet company.

Memos like this one were the working paper of the Garrison probe. Each interview was written up and passed to the district attorney, building the file behind his case. Sewell's job put him in charge of company cars, a subject the investigators wanted on record. The memo preserves one small piece of that inquiry.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ErnestBarryW_Er: Barry Ernest wrote to Harold Weisberg on November 29, 1968 with a business offer. Ernest offered to sell Weisberg copies of his books on the assassination case. The surviving record gives the date, the two men, and the offer. It does not give the titles or prices involved. The letter stands as a small piece of the trade in assassination books between researchers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HickeyGeorgeW_H:
Howard C. H. Donahue filed a defendant's memorandum supporting his motion to dismiss a lawsuit. George W. Hickey Jr. had sued him in the Circuit Court for Baltimore County, Maryland, case number 108/268/95CV3513. The memorandum sets out Donahue's legal argument for ending the case before trial.

A motion to dismiss tests whether a claim can proceed at all, and the memo is the defendant's side in writing. Court filings like this one preserve disputes in their formal shape: caption, case number, and argument. Readers get Donahue's defense as his lawyers framed it for the judge.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-McLarryRussellW:
A researcher made this note, dated October 30, 1968, about Russell W. McLarry. Time magazine reported that the Secret Service had arrested McLarry for a threat against President Johnson. The note-taker asked fellow researcher Gary Schoener to have the Archives check its files on the man.

Notes like this one were the working memory of assassination research. A magazine line raised a question; a note assigned the follow-up to a named colleague. The McLarry item joins two obsessions of the era: threats against presidents, and the fear that official files hid the pattern. The note preserves the question and the request, not the answer the Archives gave.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PlayboyWoodward:
Playboy advertised its coming two-part excerpt of 'All the President's Men,' the Watergate book by Carl Bernstein and Bob Woodward. The excerpt began with the May 1974 issue. The magazine billed it as 'the publishing event of the year.' A men's magazine buying the season's biggest political book was itself part of the event.

Watergate reporting had made the two Washington Post reporters famous before their book appeared. Serial rights let magazines print the best chapters first. Playboy's advertisement shows the book being sold as popular drama, not just journalism. It preserves the pitch and the moment: spring 1974, the scandal still unfolding, and the story of its reporting already a prize property.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-TaylorWarrenW_T: Secret Service Agent Warren W. Taylor gave a formal statement on November 29, 1963, one week after President Kennedy was killed. Taylor had served on the Vice President's detail in Dallas. His statement records what an agent on duty that day saw and did. Statements taken this soon after the event are among the closest records historians have to the day itself.
in-the-yule-log-glow-book-i-christmas-ta:
Harrison S. Morris edited In the Yule-Log Glow, Christmas tales from round the world, as Book I of three. The Philadelphia edition of 1900 reprints the 1891 copyright. Morris invites the reader to step by a ruddy fire and hear voices from many lands. A Russian, a Sicilian, a German, and a Spaniard share the hearth in his frame.

Tales in this first book turn on homecoming and duty at Christmas. Dolly welcomes her father home in one, calling a merry Christmas as wind draws tears. Fathers repeat that she is always on duty. Book I sets the warm, gathered tone of the set.
journals-of-two-expeditions-into-the-int:
John Oxley's Journals of Two Expeditions into the Interior of New South Wales record government surveys of 1817 and 1818. Oxley was surveyor general of the territory and a lieutenant of the Royal Navy. The book appeared with maps and views of the newly discovered country. Appendices print his instructions, official reports, and letters to the governor.

One appendix gives Mr. Evans's diary for part of July 1818. Others report Oxley's return and his discovery of Port Stephens. Tables of population, land under cultivation, and stock for 1813 to 1817 close the volume. The journals show exploration as official work: orders, surveys, and reports. They remain basic sources for the first opening of inland New South Wales.
journals-of-two-expeditions-of-discovery:
Volume one of George Grey's Journals of Two Expeditions of Discovery covers his travels in north-west and western Australia. The expeditions ran through 1837, 1838, and 1839, under the authority of the British government. Grey later became governor of South Australia. The London edition of 1841 fills two volumes, of which this is the first.

The title page promises many newly discovered, fertile districts described in detail. It also promises observations on the moral and physical condition of the Aboriginal inhabitants. Grey wrote as both explorer and official, judging land for settlement as he crossed it. His journals became standard reading on western Australia's coasts and peoples. This volume opens that record with the first of the two expeditions.
maxims-and-opinions-of-field-marshal-his:
George Henry Francis edited the Maxims and Opinions of the Duke of Wellington. Henry Colburn printed the book in London in 1845. It draws on Wellington's writings and speeches across more than fifty years.

A short life of the duke stands at the front of the book. The editor says most past works stress the duke's wars alone. His years as a minister and statesman, he argues, got far less care. These pages let readers judge Wellington's claims in that second, civic life. The duke's own words, not tales about him, fill most pages. Readers can weigh his views on war, rule, and public duty.
podcast-joerogan-qDkHCaNAo_w:
Historian Rebecca Lemov joins Joe Rogan for episode 2322 to talk about mind control. Lemov studies the history of brainwashing claims and the science used to back them. Her work runs from Cold War labs to cults and interrogation rooms.

Lemov traces how brainwashing became a household fear during the Cold War. She describes real experiments on sleep, drugs, and isolation, and how courts and media used the idea. Rogan asks what actually works and what is myth. The episode gives a careful history of a word people still throw around loosely today.
talbot-mundy-biblio-materials-toward-a-b:
Materials Toward a Bibliography of the Works of Talbot Mundy, edited by Bradford M. Day, opens with a short life of the adventure novelist. Mundy was born in London on April 23, 1879, educated at Rugby, and spent nearly ten years, from 1900, in government service across Africa and India.

Day tells how Mundy rode all over India. He rode even into Tibet. He absorbed eastern occult lore until it fascinated him. Then he studied the nature magic of East African tribes at first hand. He travelled through Egypt, the Near East, and parts of Arabia. He killed dozens of lions and hunted ivory. Arriving in the United States in 1911, he stayed, took citizenship, and turned to writing, placing Pig-Sticking in India in Adventure magazine that April. The bibliography that follows serves collectors of his eastern adventure tales.
the-discipline-of-war-nine-addresses-on-: The Rev. J. Hasloch Potter, canon of Southwark and vicar of St. Mark's, Surbiton, published The Discipline of War with Skeffington and Son of London in 1915. The subtitle promises nine addresses on the lessons of the war in connection with Lent, from Ash Wednesday to Easter Sunday. In his preface Potter says the war has brought new conditions into lives. The addresses, written amid much other pressing work, offer simple hints for conduct and points for thought. Only the title page and that preface are present here.
the-fifteen-decisive-battles-of-the-worl:
Sir Edward Creasy picked fifteen battles he judged to have changed the course of the world, from Marathon to Waterloo. His book on them, by a former chief justice of Ceylon, became a famed work of plain history.

In his preface Creasy grants that war is a sad need, to be used only in self-defense when peace talks fail. Yet he says great battles draw us by the courage and skill shown in them. Each fight is told, then weighed for what hung on its outcome: the fate of Greece, of Rome, of England, and of free states yet unborn.
the-fugitive-blacksmith-or-events-in-the:
James W. C. Pennington wrote The Fugitive Blacksmith as the tale of his own life, from slave in Maryland to pastor of a Presbyterian church in New York. This second edition was printed at London in 1849.

Pennington thanks the British public in a letter from Hoxton, dated October 15, 1849, for calling for a new edition so soon. He credits kind reviews in the press for much of the book's reach. His tale tells of his youth in bondage, his flight north, his schooling, and his rise to the pulpit. Such slave tales gave British and American readers a first-hand voice against bondage.
the-paths-of-inland-commerce-a-chronicle:
Archer B. Hulbert wrote The Paths of Inland Commerce, a chronicle of trail, road, and waterway, as volume 21 of the Chronicles of America series. Yale University Press published it in 1920, in the Abraham Lincoln edition, with Allen Johnson as editor. Hulbert's preface, signed from Worcester, Massachusetts, guesses that the great American novel, if written, will turn on transportation.

Every problem in building the republic, he argues, was at bottom a problem in transportation. He pictures the rivalries of pack-horseman and wagoner, riverman and canal boatman, steamboat promoter and railway capitalist. Each new way met scorn from the old, from wagoners deriding Clinton's Ditch to boatmen wanting to ram Fulton's Clermont.
the-prose-works-of-jonathan-swift-d-d-vo:
Volume X of Swift's Prose Works, the Historical Writings, was edited by Temple Scott and published in 1902. An editorial note discusses the manuscript of Swift's History, collated by Percy Fitzgerald against the Lucas version. Fitzgerald himself, forty-five years on, cannot recall making the collation, a lapse the editor regrets. If the manuscript is what it claims, the note says, authenticity is settled for ever, and the present edition records its corrections and variations.

Lord Orrery's 1752 Remarks on Swift drew severe censure from the author's surviving friends. Whatever Orrery's private opinion, the editor allows, his facts deserve hearing. Orrery wrote that Swift left few manuscripts of consequence, one exception being his account of the peace of Utrecht. Swift called it An History of the Four Last Years of Queen Anne.
the-system-of-nature-or-the-laws-of-the-:
Paul Henri Thiery, Baron d'Holbach, wrote this system of nature. It was first published in French under the name Mirabaud in 1770. Samuel Wilkinson's English translation of 1820 and 1821 appears here. This is volume one of two. Production notes explain the facsimile source, and a contents page promises laws of nature and of man, the faculties of the soul, the doctrine of immortality, and happiness.

Chapter one opens with a chain of flat assertions. Man deceives himself whenever he abandons experience for imaginary systems. Nature made him, the chapter says. He exists in nature and is subject to her laws. He cannot free himself from them. He cannot step beyond them even in thought. That uncompromising materialism drives the whole treatise on the moral and physical world.
